issues.issue: The extension operates only "to the extent such Collective Bargaining Agreement is not modified by, or inconsistent with" the Memorandum, but the Memorandum supplies no rule for deciding when a CBA term is "inconsistent" with it. Which of the two instruments controls on any disputed subject is therefore left to construction.

A "restated commitment" to "orderly, successful and efficient start-up and operations" states no measurable obligation and no consequence for failure. Whether it is an operative promise or mere preamble is open.

The "commitment to negotiate those issues arising out of the start-up and operations" at other facilities fixes no subject matter, timetable or standard of good faith. It is an agreement to agree whose enforceable content is undefined.

This clause applies the contract at "any new or rebuilt facility," but the May 16, 1992 side letter (c074) removes 43rd Street and the staging facility from all references to "new and rebuilt facilities." The two must be reconciled to know where the Memorandum-as-modified operates.

The permitted Edison practices are described generally ("technological innovations, methods of operation, scheduling practices and/or working conditions") and then illustrated by "e.g. palletization, tractor-trailer delivery to wholesalers, and card reader system." Whether the general words are confined to matters of the kind enumerated is a classic ejusdem generis question.

"[A]fter a period of 120 days" has no stated starting event — notice, commencement of negotiations, or announcement of the innovation. The trigger for compulsory interest arbitration is therefore indeterminate.

The paragraph is headed "The Contract Arbitrator" but its text terminates the "Merits Arbitrator," and "contract year" is nowhere defined. Which office may be terminated, and in what annual window, is uncertain on the face of the clause.

The Merits Arbitrator is given all grievance jurisdiction "except as otherwise provided herein," yet paragraph 7C (c033) preserves the Joint Standing Committee, Adjustment Board and Appeal Board as the deciding tribunals, and paragraph 2 also keeps a Status Quo Arbitrator. Which forum hears a given dispute cannot be settled from this clause alone.
No period is fixed within which the parties must "fail to reach agreement" before the AAA rules take over. When either side may invoke the AAA procedure is left open.

The clause selects a new Status Quo Arbitrator "pursuant to the procedure described in paragraph B above," but section 2 of the Memorandum contains no lettered paragraph B. The cross-reference is a mechanical error that leaves the selection procedure unidentified.
"[A]ll active NMDU RSHs employed by the Times" turns on the undefined word "active," which fixes no date and no employment status test. Who is inside the buyout class is therefore contestable.

This definition requires presence on the Group I list both at signing and at ratification, while Attachment B's eligibility clause (c053) requires only that the individual be on the list "effective the date of ratification." The two eligibility tests cannot both govern the same buyout class.

"[T]hese contributions shall be in lieu of and not in addition to those that would otherwise be called for by the Agreement" does not say whether the 450-FTE figure is a floor only, or also a ceiling displacing the CBA's per-shift-worked contribution obligation. The phrase governs the size of the employer's whole welfare obligation and reads both ways.

The clause fixes only that contributions are "based on the highest straight time scale" but states no number of shifts or weeks per year for employees who are no longer working. The amount of the post-buyout pension contribution is therefore not computable from the text.

The 45-day window commences "promptly after ratification," which fixes no date certain for the opening or closing of the offer. Later provisions (c026, c027) key operational rights to "closure of the forty-five (45) day buyout offer period," so the vagueness propagates.

The Times must add employees "necessary to reach 370 regular situations" but the only permitted source is Eligible Group I Employees who decline the buyout, a pool that may be too small. The clause does not say what happens if 370 cannot be reached from that source.

The 270-RSH floor applies only "[o]nce the replacement procedure has been completed," but the paragraph gives the procedure no completion event — it runs "during the term of this Agreement." When the floor attaches is therefore indeterminate.

The duty to replace absent RSHs turns on whether reporting numbers are "insufficient to satisfy specific manning requirements," a term used repeatedly but nowhere defined in the Memorandum. Whose manning standard governs is left open.

Promotion is required only where "necessary to comply ... with specific manning requirements," an undefined benchmark. The circumstances triggering a mandatory promotion cannot be identified from the text.

"[F]ollowing discussion with the Union" imposes a precondition of unspecified content, timing or effect before The Times exercises its discretion. Whether a single notice satisfies it, and what follows if it does not occur, is unstated.

The proviso barring consolidation of situations "in which one run constitutes the entire day's or night's work for a shift on three or more shifts each week" is opaque as to what counts as "one run" and how shifts are counted. The scope of the limit on consolidation is the whole of its content.

The clause permits reorganization of "all existing daily West Side Direct routes, including both daily and Sunday routes" and then a "fifty percent (50%)" reduction yielding exactly thirteen routes, figures that do not reconcile with treating Sunday routes as part of the daily total. Whether the 50% cap or the fixed route/assignment numbers controls is ambiguous.

The reorganization is stated to be "subject only to the limitation" of a forty-route minimum, yet the May 16, 1992 Saturday Night Bulldog letter (c075) imposes a further limitation freezing forty current finishing times. The word "only" cannot be squared with that letter.

Moving SNBD start times to no later than 4:00 p.m. after Edison opens sits against the side letter (c075) freezing the forty current finishing times for those routes. Whether shift length may be lengthened, or the finishing times move with the start times, is unresolved between the two.
"[D]aily Bulldog routes" is not defined and its boundary against the separately treated Saturday Night Bulldog routes is unclear. Whether Saturday routes count toward the two/four minima is open.

Cash collections continue "on recovery routes," a category the Memorandum never defines, and the permitted "alternate billing system" is left wholly unspecified. The boundary between eliminated and continued collections is uncertain.

After enumerating strikes, job actions and acts honoring picket lines against named categories, the clause sweeps in "any other acts that interfere with the Publisher's operations or the production or sale of its products or services." How far that catch-all extends beyond the enumerated kinds of conduct is an ejusdem generis question.

Release is available "after five (5) working days," but the saving proviso measures the non-complying party's time to move to vacate by "that five (5) day period." The two counting rules are inconsistent within one sentence.

The release mechanism runs off awards of the Joint Standing Committee, Adjustment Board and Appeal Board, while paragraph 2 (c008) vests all grievance resolution in the Merits Arbitrator "except as otherwise provided herein." Whether a Merits Arbitrator award triggers this release cannot be answered from either clause alone.

The clause states a fixed resulting scale of $952.80, but the cost-of-living provision (c040) directs adjustments "beginning on March 31, 1992" on a new January-to-January index. The stated dollar result and the COLA-adjusted scale cannot both be true.

A resulting scale of $986.80 is fixed for March 31, 1994, the same date on which c040 requires a cost-of-living adjustment to the scale. Whether the COLA is on top of, or already embedded in, the stated figure is unresolved between the two clauses.

A resulting scale of $1020.80 is fixed for March 31, 1995, while c040 requires a cost-of-living adjustment effective the same date. The stated figure and the COLA provision cannot both be applied without construction.

The reopener sends "the matter" to binding arbitration without saying whether the arbitrator's remit is wages alone or the whole reopener package, and "the then current scale" is not fixed to a date. The scope of the interest arbitration is therefore contestable.

The sentence is grammatically incomplete — "reapportion the contributions due on those increases between its pension plan and its health and welfare plan the total pension (8%) and health and welfare (7.68%) plan contributions made by The Times" — so it cannot be told whether the Union may reapportion only the contributions attributable to the wage increases or the entire 15.68% of contributions. The missing words are the whole subject of the right conferred.

A reapportionment that raises the welfare percentage sits against paragraph 3.A.(3) (c015), which fixes health and welfare contributions at a 450-Full-Time-Equivalent minimum "in lieu of and not in addition to" what the Agreement would otherwise require. How a percentage-based reapportionment operates on an FTE-based fixed obligation is not addressed.

The clause lists adjustment dates beginning March 31, 1994 but the proviso speaks of "all such adjustments beginning on March 31, 1992," a date not in the list, and omits March 31, 1996 altogether. The internal mismatch leaves the set of adjusted years uncertain.

Ratification is required "by each of the parties" with no deadline, no procedure and no statement of what happens if one party fails to ratify. Because the buyout periods and other obligations run from ratification, the omission has operative consequences.

Attachment A limits eligibility to RSHs on the "Steady Situation list ... currently holding positions," while paragraph 3.A of the Memorandum (c011) offers the buyout to "all active NMDU RSHs employed by the Times, including foremen." The two eligibility descriptions do not coincide, and the Memorandum says the Attachments contain the governing terms.
"[I]nterest at prevailing market interest rates" fixes no index, term or measuring date for the annuity purchase. The value of the alternative to a lump sum is therefore indeterminate.

The unpaid balance is directed to "the employee's estate," but the Notice of Termination form the employee must sign (c052) invites him to name a person to whom "the remaining amount of my buyout shall be paid." Estate versus named designee cannot both control the same balance.

The cross-reference to "Paragraph 3-A-(3) and 3-A-(5)" is unreliable because the subparagraphs of paragraph 3.A are mis-numbered in the Memorandum (the sequence runs 1), 2), 3), then 5), 6), 7)). Which numbered promises this Attachment incorporates has to be worked out against c015 and c017.

The employee is made to surrender "his or her contractual guarantee of employment," a guarantee this Attachment never identifies — it may mean the Appendix A employment guarantees, the CBA's job security, or both. What is being given up is left to construction.
The 45-day period runs "promptly after ratification of this Agreement," fixing neither the opening date nor the closing date of the offer. "Promptly" is the only measure supplied.

The acceptance form describes the Memorandum of Agreement as "dated December , 1991," whereas the Memorandum was made and executed in May 1992 (c061 and the letters are dated May 16, 1992). The mis-dating leaves it uncertain which instrument the employee is accepting a buyout under.

The form lets the employee designate a person to receive the remaining buyout amount, while Attachment A, Schedule of Payments 3 (c045) directs the unpaid balance to the employee's estate. The designation and the estate provision cannot both govern.

Attachment B extends the offer to those on the Group I list "effective the date of ratification," while the Memorandum's definition (c014) requires presence on the list both at signing and at ratification. The two eligibility tests differ for the same group.
"[I]nterest at prevailing market interest rates" identifies no rate source, annuity term or measurement date. The economic content of the annuity election is unfixed.

The balance goes to "the individual's estate," but the Attachment B Notice of Termination (c060) invites the individual to name someone to whom the remaining buyout is to be paid. The two payment directions conflict.
The offer stays open 45 days "commencing promptly after ratification," which supplies no ascertainable opening or closing date. "Promptly" is the only measure of the trigger.

The Attachment B acceptance form refers to a Memorandum of Agreement "dated December , 1991," while the Memorandum bears a May 1992 date. The date is a mechanical error about the very instrument being accepted.
The beneficiary designation on the form conflicts with Attachment B, Schedule of Payments 3 (c056), which directs any unpaid balance to the individual's estate. Which controls on death is unresolved.

Guaranteed Employees are "those Regular Situation Holders to be identified on Attachments '1' and '2'," lists that are neither annexed nor described by any criterion. The class of beneficiaries of the employment guarantee is left to be created after the fact.

"[G]uaranteed the opportunity to work five straight time shifts per week" does not say whether the guarantee is one of pay when work is not offered or merely of an offer the employee must accept. "Opportunity" carries both meanings and fixes the guarantee's value.

Appendix A repeatedly says "this Agreement," which may mean Appendix A itself or the Memorandum it is appended to, and the same sentence makes the guarantee both effective on completion of Memorandum paragraph 4B and surviving "the expiration of this Agreement." Which instrument's expiration is meant decides how long the Attachment "1" guarantees run.

The Attachment "2" guarantee ends at "the expiration date of the current Collective Bargaining Agreement," a phrase that may mean the March 30, 1993 expiry recited in the opening clause (c001) or that Agreement as there extended to March 30, 2000. The guarantee's duration turns entirely on that term.

The right to "utilize fully" Guaranteed Employees "in inverse seniority order" before hiring others sits against paragraph B (c062), which guarantees each Guaranteed Employee five straight-time shifts a week. Calling up the most junior first can leave senior guaranteed employees short of their guarantee.

Guarantees are confined to persons listed on Attachments "1" and "2" "except for Eligible Group I Employees who obtain guarantees pursuant to paragraph 4B" of the Memorandum, while paragraph 4B (c021) says those employees' guarantee is "governed by the terms of Appendix A" — which limits itself to the listed individuals. The two provisions refer to each other without fixing the content of the Group I guarantee.

Suspension of the guarantee depends on the delivery department's operations being suspended "in circumstances under which RSH's are not entitled to be paid under the Collective Bargaining Agreement," a condition defined only by an external document not reproduced here. Which shutdowns qualify cannot be determined from this instrument.

"[P]ermanent suspension of the Newspaper" identifies neither the publication nor who determines permanence, and no notice or verification mechanism is supplied. A prolonged but arguably temporary shutdown falls in the gap.

The general words are "any employee who terminates employment for any reason," yet the enumerated instances include discharge, death and permanent disability — none of them acts of the employee. The list contradicts the general term it is said to illustrate.

The Times may terminate the guarantees for "any violation" of the No-Strike clause, while paragraph 7C of the Memorandum (c033) expressly releases the Union from that clause on the employer's non-compliance with an award. A work stoppage lawful under 7C would still forfeit the guarantees under this clause.

The Union's option is triggered by a "wage package" agreed with another union, and the letter never says whether pension and welfare contributions form part of a "wage package." The predecessor 1987 provision used "wage and benefit package," making the narrowed term's scope a live question.

The right is triggered by agreement with "any labor organization" followed by a closed parenthetical list of nine named unions. Whether the parenthetical exhausts the trigger or merely illustrates it is a general-versus-specific problem.

Disputes go to "the Contract's grievance and arbitration procedure," while paragraph 2 of the Memorandum (c008) vests all disputes over the Agreement in the Merits Arbitrator selected under its own procedure. Which machinery hears a most-favored-wage dispute is unsettled between the two.

The Times must file the vacatur papers "promptly upon notification" of ratification, with no outside date and no specified form of notification. What counts as prompt, and as notification, is left open.

This letter excludes 43rd Street and the staging facility from every reference to "new and rebuilt facilities," while paragraph 1A of the Memorandum (c004) applies the contract as modified at "any new or rebuilt facility" within the NMDU's jurisdiction. The scope of section 1 cannot be fixed without reconciling the two.

The letter freezes forty current SNBD finishing times "throughout the duration of this contract," while paragraph 6 of the Memorandum (c027) makes the reorganization "subject only to" the forty-route minimum. The letter adds a limitation that paragraph 6 says does not exist.

The letter funds welfare shortfalls out of the paragraph 3.A.(3) contributions and then requires "additional contributions" if those are insufficient, whereas paragraph 3.A.(3) (c015) states that its contributions are "in lieu of and not in addition to" what the Agreement would otherwise require. Whether The Times owes more than the 450-FTE minimum turns on reconciling them.

The obligation is measured by "shift contributions needed to maintain benefit status," a standard set by the Pension Fund's own rules and nowhere stated in this instrument. The size of the employer's separate contribution is not ascertainable from the letter.

The whole funding obligation is conditioned on the individuals' "willingness ... to avail themselves of all work opportunities that may exist at The New York Times," a condition with no test, no procedure for proving it, and no indication whether one refusal defeats the obligation for all. "All work opportunities" is also unbounded as to location, shift and classification.

The letter raises the minimum FTE contributions by the number of FTEs employed "in excess of 370," while paragraph 3-A(3) (c015) sets the minimum at 450 FTEs — so employment of, say, 400 FTEs would produce a 480-FTE contribution obligation. How the 370 threshold works against the 450 floor is not explained.

Dedicated school and college drivers are assigned "a regular shift time of 2:30 to 9:30 a.n.," yet on suspension or abolition of the route "the driver's start time will revert to 11:30 p.m." — a time the clause never established. What the driver reverts to, and on what notice, is unclear.

"[E]very effort within its control" to protect the NMDU's jurisdiction against "hootlegging" operations supplies neither a standard of effort nor a definition of the target conduct. Both the obligation and its object are undefined.
The committee is composed of two representatives from each side with no chair, tie-breaker or decision rule. Deadlock is unaddressed and the committee's output is not made binding on anyone.

The committee is "specifically charged with administering the transfer process," without saying whether that gives it authority to decide transfers or only to implement decisions The Times makes. "Administering" carries both meanings against the Times' discretion elsewhere in the package.

The 1996 contributions are reduced from the 450-FTE obligation and "[s]aid reductions will be evenly distributed throughout the calendar years 1992, 1993, 1994, and 1995" — reductions to years that will already have closed before the 1996 contributions are made. How a future measurement is spread over past contribution years is not explained.

The reduction cuts into the 450-Full-Time-Equivalent minimum fixed by paragraph 3-A(3) (c015), which is expressed as a firm minimum for 1992-1995. Whether the minimum or the reduction controls those years is a direct clash.

The parties promise to "take the steps necessary to effectuate amendments to the Health and Welfare Plan" required by paragraph 3-A(3) (c015), but the Plan is a trusteed fund whose contributions are set by the collective bargaining agreements and trust instrument, not by these two parties. What amendments are "necessitated," and whether the promisors can deliver them, only appears when the instruments are read together.

The clause turns on "the most junior qualified situation holder" without any definition of "qualified" or of the pool from which juniority is measured. Who may be compelled to take an Edison situation is therefore contestable.

This paragraph requires at least four days' notice before assignment, while the following paragraph (c088) requires the Chapel Chairman to produce a volunteer within three days and the volunteer to fill the situation within seven days of notification. The two timetables cannot be run together for the same vacancy.

The volunteer procedure must precede the junior-assignment procedure, yet its three-day and seven-day steps are inconsistent with the four days' notice that c087 requires before a junior holder is assigned, and it ends by permanently assigning the junior holder anyway. Sequencing the two paragraphs requires construction.

The exception depends on a vacancy "foreseen to be of two (2) weeks or less duration," without saying by whom the foresight is exercised or what happens when it proves wrong. The exception is thus effectively self-judged.

The Times is given a bare "option to fill any vacancies created" by a junior assignment, while the same letter (c086) commits the parties to staff vacant, newly created or temporary situations expeditiously. Whether the option overrides that commitment for the knock-on vacancy is unaddressed.

The NMDU "may, within 72 hours, discuss the possibility of employment opportunities," without identifying what event starts the 72 hours or imposing any duty on The Times beyond discussion. Both the trigger and the substance of the right are indeterminate.

The award of a named dispatcher position to M. Santor by side letter sits against the bidding and seniority-based assignment machinery preserved elsewhere in the package (c086-c088 and the Contract's bid procedures). Whether other situation holders' bid rights yield to this individual award is not addressed.
The letter commits M. Santor to withdraw his grievance "with prejudice" although he is not a signatory to it and no mechanism binds him. Who must act, and what follows if he does not, is unstated.
